cards.title: Anthropic raises $81.3 billion in the largest IPO on record

visual.label: Raised by Anthropic at $83 a share, above its $70 to $78 range

cards.what: Anthropic sold about 980 million shares at $83, valuing it near $1.5 trillion fully diluted. Trading starts Thursday on Nasdaq as ANT.
cards.why: A major AI supplier now reports to public investors, so its prices, spending and risks get quarterly scrutiny.
cards.say: Which of our AI contracts depend on Anthropic, and what changes now it reports every quarter?
deeper: CNBC reports the deal was upsized and beat SpaceX's June IPO, which raised $75 billion at first and $85.7 billion in total once underwriters sold extra shares. That extra-share step is today's term of the day.

Reports say each of the seven co-founders sold nearly 3.4 million shares. Watch the first trade on Thursday and whether underwriters sell extra shares, which would lift the total raised. Some early reports cited people familiar with the matter.

cards.title: Palo Alto pays $4.5 billion for a 50-person AI startup

visual.label: All-stock price Palo Alto Networks agreed to pay for Applied Compute

cards.what: Applied Compute helps firms train custom open-weight AI models and agents. Founded in May 2025, it reports about $100 million in annualised revenue.
cards.why: Security vendors are buying AI skills to protect models firms run themselves. The price shows how scarce that talent is.
cards.say: Who secures the open-weight models we run ourselves, and is it on our security vendor's roadmap?
deeper: The price is about $1.25 billion above the $3.25 billion valuation Applied Compute set weeks earlier, when it raised $350 million. Palo Alto expects the unit to add more than $1 billion of security annual recurring revenue by 2029. CEO Yash Patil, an OpenAI alumnus, becomes co-chief AI officer.

Palo Alto announced the deal with results: quarterly revenue of $3.44 billion beat forecasts and shares rose over 7% after hours. Closing needs regulatory clearance. The revenue target is the buyer's own forecast.

cards.title: Fed minutes: almost all officials see more rate hikes ahead

visual.label: October vote to hold US rates at 3.75% to 4%; two wanted a hike

cards.what: Minutes of the October meeting show almost all officials expect further hikes. Two said December could need more than a quarter point.
cards.why: Higher US rates lift borrowing costs worldwide and strengthen the dollar, squeezing emerging market currencies and growth plans.
cards.say: If US rates rise again in December, which of our plans assume cheap capital?
deeper: The two who voted for a hike in October were Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack. The minutes did not name the two officials who floated a bigger December move. Markets now price a December hike; the Fed meets on 8 and 9 December.
The news hit the Dow and gold on Wednesday, and the S&P 500 fell below its 200-day average, a level traders watch for trend breaks.

cards.title: Microsoft and Salesforce put CRM inside Copilot; prices stay unknown

visual.label: Prebuilt sales skills in the Salesforce in Copilot plugin, now in preview

cards.what: Copilotforce brings Salesforce data and sales workflows into Copilot, Teams and Fabric, with data shared between both platforms without copying it.
cards.why: Agents may live where staff already work, not inside each app. Control splits: Salesforce governs CRM access, Microsoft its compliance.
cards.say: Before any pilot, ask who owns the agent, who pays both licences, and who audits changes it writes.
deeper: The firms announced Copilotforce at Microsoft Ignite on 17 November. Teams support is still in pilot. Changes written back to the CRM need explicit user confirmation. Accenture is the design partner and calls itself customer zero.
Pricing, required licences and regional dates were not disclosed. These are vendor announcements reported by trade press, so treat the claims as plans until general availability.

cards.title: Textron sells its industrial arm for $1.2 billion to focus on aerospace

visual.label: Price Kingswood Capital agreed to pay for Textron's Industrial segment

cards.what: Textron is selling Kautex fuel systems and its specialised vehicles unit, including E-Z-GO golf carts, to private equity firm Kingswood.
cards.why: Leadership is solving for focus: a pure aerospace and defence group is simpler for investors to value and managers to run.
cards.say: Which of our units would a buyer value more than we do? That is the divestment test.
deeper: Textron expects about $1.1 billion after tax and costs, and a noncash charge of $350 million to $400 million this quarter. Closing is expected in the first half of 2027. What remains is Textron Aviation, Bell and Textron Systems.

Reuters notes the sale follows an April plan to separate the unit and last year's sale of the powersports business. A new buyback of up to 35 million shares suggests some proceeds go back to shareholders.

cards.title: India's goods trade gap hits a 12-month high of $39.88 billion

visual.title: India goods trade, October 2026, $ billion (Commerce Ministry)

cards.what: Fuel pushed goods imports to a record $89.35 billion in October. Exports rose 45% to $49.47 billion. Services narrowed the total gap to $20.09 billion.
cards.why: A wide goods gap pressures the rupee and imported inflation, which already sits above the RBI's limit.
cards.say: How much of our cost base is priced in dollars or tied to fuel, and is it hedged?
deeper: Services, including IT and other business services, did the heavy lifting: estimated exports of $40.51 billion against imports of $20.72 billion. The October services figures are estimates, because the latest RBI data covers September.

Over April to October the combined deficit widened by $10.10 billion. Business Standard links much of the rise in both exports and imports to higher energy prices. The data were released on 13 November.

cards.title: Winner's curse: the top bidder often paid too much

items.label: Uncertain value
items.note: No one knows the true worth.

items.label: Highest guess wins
items.note: The winner is often the most optimistic.

cards.what: When many bidders guess an uncertain value, the winner is usually the one who guessed highest, so winning often means overpaying.
cards.why: Use it for acquisitions, talent bidding wars, auctions and any contest where the prize's value is unclear.
cards.say: On our next bid, ask: if we win, what did we see that every rival missed?
deeper: Three Atlantic Richfield engineers, Ed Capen, Bob Clapp and Bill Campbell, named it in a 1971 paper, Competitive Bidding in High-Risk Situations. They argued oil firms earned poor returns on Gulf of Mexico lease auctions because winners overestimated reserves.
The curse grows with uncertainty and with the number of bidders. The fix is not to stop bidding but to adjust your estimate for the fact that you won.

sources.title: AAPG Explorer: Bid winners can face 'curse'

cards.title: MBA students paid $10.01 for jars worth $8

visual.label: Average winning bid for a jar of coins worth $8.00

cards.what: In 1983, Bazerman and Samuelson auctioned jars of coins to MBA students. The winning bid averaged $10.01, a $2.01 loss per winner.
cards.why: Smart people overpay when value is uncertain and rivals are many. Experience alone does not cure it.
cards.say: Palo Alto paid $1.25 billion over a weeks-old valuation. What would make us walk away?
deeper: Max Bazerman and William Samuelson ran the auctions in 12 Boston University classes and published the results in the Journal of Conflict Resolution. Richard Thaler later summarised the jar result in a 1988 review of the winner's curse.
The link to today's Palo Alto deal is an illustration, not a verdict. A strategic buyer may know things rivals do not, which is the honest test for any premium.

cards.title: TPUs are Google's own chips, built only for AI maths

items.label: AI is maths
items.note: Models are mostly huge grids of multiplication.

items.label: Custom chip
items.note: A TPU does that maths and little else.

items.label: Linked pods
items.note: Ironwood joins up to 9,216 chips as one.

items.label: Rented capacity
items.note: Firms rent TPU time through Google Cloud.

cards.what: A TPU is a chip Google designed for the maths inside AI models. Unlike a GPU, it trades flexibility for speed and lower cost.
cards.why: TPUs give Google a cost lever that Nvidia buyers lack, and give customers a second source of AI compute.
cards.say: Ask your cloud team what it would take to run one of our models on TPUs.
deeper: Ironwood is the seventh generation, listed as TPU7x. Google's documentation gives each chip 192 GiB of fast memory and a peak of 4,614 trillion operations a second at low precision. A full pod of 9,216 chips draws nearly 10 megawatts.
Peak figures are Google's own and real speed depends on software. Code written for Nvidia's CUDA tools does not move over for free, which is the hidden switching cost.

cards.title: Jobs cut Apple to four product lines and returned it to profit

visual.label: Apple's fiscal 1998 profit, a year after losing over $1 billion

cards.what: Back as interim CEO in 1997, Jobs drew a two by two grid: consumer or pro, desktop or portable. About 70% of products went.
cards.why: Apple swung from a loss of about $1 billion in fiscal 1997 to a $309 million profit in fiscal 1998.
cards.say: Focus is subtraction. Name one product or project we would cut if we could only keep four.
deeper: Accounts say Apple sold more than 15 computer platforms before the cut and four after. Jobs also secured a $150 million investment from Microsoft in 1997, and the iMac launched in 1998.
Caveat: sources differ on the 1997 loss, from $816 million to $1.045 billion, depending on the period counted. The turnaround had several causes, so do not credit the grid alone.

cards.title: Porter's What Is Strategy?: choosing what not to do
cards.what: Doing the same things better than rivals is operational effectiveness, not strategy. Strategy means different activities, and trade-offs about what to leave out.
cards.why: It separates improvement programmes from real strategic choices, and gives leaders a test for vague plans.
cards.say: If our plan has no trade-offs, it is an improvement list, not a strategy.
deeper: Michael Porter published the article in Harvard Business Review in November 1996. He uses firms such as IKEA and Vanguard to show how trade-offs and fit across activities make a position hard to copy. It pairs well with today's Textron and Apple stories.

sources.title: Porter (1996): What Is Strategy?, Harvard Business Review reprint

cards.title: Greenshoe option

visual.label: Typical extra shares underwriters may sell in an IPO

cards.what: An IPO clause letting underwriters sell about 15% more shares than planned, then buy them from the issuer or the market.
cards.why: Anthropic's record IPO may get bigger if underwriters use it, as SpaceX's did in June.
cards.say: Is that the headline raise, or the total after the greenshoe?
deeper: Underwriters oversell the deal, then cover. If the price falls, they buy shares in the market, which supports the price. If it rises, they buy extra shares from the company at the IPO price. The option usually runs about 30 days. The name comes from Green Shoe Manufacturing, the first firm to use it, in 1963 by Bloomberg's account.

question.text: Palo Alto paid $1.25 billion above a weeks-old valuation for AI talent. What would make us walk away from a deal?
question.context: Prompted by the Applied Compute deal and the winner's curse. Agreeing a walk-away price before bidding starts is the simplest guard against overpaying in a hot market.
